entries.falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA Data Center revenue (D2) falls quarter over quarter, or CoWoS lead times drop below 12 weeks.
entries.mechanism: Memory and packaging shortages cap how many GPUs NVIDIA can build while customers keep ordering more, so demand runs ahead of supply.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to how fast memory and packaging capacity catch up to order volume.
entries.statement: Datacenter GPU demand continues to outrun NVIDIA's ability to serve it.
entries.title: NVDA demand durability

entries.falsifiableTrigger: HBM4 contract prices (hbmSupplyCapex) fall quarter over quarter and HBM3E/HBM4 stop being sold out before 2027.
entries.mechanism: Memory makers cannot expand high-bandwidth memory fast enough, so it now sets the ceiling on how many accelerators vendors can build and sell.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to how fast memory makers add high-bandwidth memory output relative to accelerator demand.
entries.statement: High-bandwidth memory, not advanced packaging, is now the supply that caps how much merchant-GPU revenue vendors can book. Packaging is easing as the TSMC CoWoS gap narrows from about 20% to 10% by end 2026 and ASE and Hanmi add capacity, and NVIDIA's supply commitments run to $119.0B-$145B, while HBM3E/HBM4 stay sold out through 2027 with demand far above supply.
entries.title: Supply constraint binding

entries.falsifiableTrigger: AMD Data Center revenue growth (D2) stalls below the prior quarter, or its accelerator market-share-pct fails to rise above 7% within 4 quarters.
entries.mechanism: AMD is landing large multi-year orders from Meta, OpenAI and cloud providers that turn its Instinct roadmap into booked datacenter revenue.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether marquee wins convert into repeat volume orders rather than one-off deployments.
entries.statement: AMD converts its Instinct roadmap into material datacenter share.
entries.title: AMD credible second source

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Custom-ASIC share of AI accelerators (market-share-pct) stops rising above 28%, or ASIC unit growth falls below merchant-GPU growth in a year.
entries.mechanism: Hyperscalers ship their own inference chips and Broadcom-designed accelerators faster than merchant GPUs grow, taking a rising slice of new AI compute.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether captive chips stay in-house or absorb workloads that would otherwise buy merchant GPUs.
entries.statement: Hyperscaler custom silicon meaningfully displaces merchant-GPU demand growth.
entries.title: Custom ASIC substitution

entries.falsifiableTrigger: gpuSpotPrice for H100 or H200 falls more than 15% quarter over quarter as new supply lands.
entries.mechanism: Tight memory and packaging supply keeps GPUs scarce, so rental and resale prices stay high even as new capacity arrives.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to how much new capacity lands relative to demand over the next few quarters.
entries.statement: GPU rental/spot price levels hold up despite added supply.
entries.title: Pricing power persistence

entries.falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA China exportControlExposure revenue recovers above its year-earlier $9,659M level, or H200 licenses book material revenue within 2 quarters.
entries.mechanism: US license rules, tariffs and enforcement keep NVIDIA and AMD largely out of China datacenter compute, cutting a large slice of addressable demand.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether case-by-case licenses convert into booked China shipments.
entries.statement: Export-control policy materially constrains addressable merchant-GPU demand.
entries.title: Export control exposure

entries.falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA vendor-financed commitments (rpoBacklog) exceed the ~210,000-GPU level, or a financed neocloud misses payment within 4 quarters.
entries.mechanism: NVIDIA guarantees GPU purchases and rents back idle capacity for revenue share, so a growing part of its reported demand rests on credit it extends itself.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether financed neoclouds can pay from real end-customer revenue rather than more NVIDIA credit.
entries.statement: NVIDIA's own revenue-sharing and credit-support financing increasingly underwrites its accelerator demand, coupling reported demand strength to NVIDIA-extended credit and adding circularity risk to buildout durability.
entries.title: Vendor-financed demand circularity

entries.falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA's top-customer customerConcentration share rises above 22% next fiscal year, or the top three exceed 60% in a quarter.
entries.mechanism: A handful of hyperscalers supply most of NVIDIA's revenue, so one of them slowing orders or moving to in-house chips would dent demand sharply.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the largest customers keep buying merchant GPUs or shift budget to their own silicon.
entries.statement: NVIDIA's data-center revenue is increasingly concentrated in a few direct customers, raising demand-durability risk if any single hyperscaler slows orders or shifts to in-house silicon.
entries.title: Customer concentration risk

entries.falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA loses its data-center Ethernet switch revenue lead (market-share-pct) within 2 quarters.
entries.mechanism: NVIDIA sells its Spectrum-X and Quantum networking bundled with Blackwell systems, so buyers adopting its GPUs also take its switches, raising switching costs.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether open Ethernet rivals can unbundle networking from the GPU purchase.
entries.statement: NVIDIA now leads the data-center Ethernet switch market and sells that networking bundled with its GPUs, deepening a full-system moat that raises switching costs versus standalone accelerators and custom chips. NVIDIA took the top revenue spot in data-center Ethernet switching in Q1 2026 by pairing Spectrum-X and Quantum with Blackwell and GB300, and its NVLink systems cut cost per token, but no finding compares networking growth against compute growth, so the sharper claim that networking scales faster than compute is not supported.
entries.title: Networking attach as systems moat

entries.falsifiableTrigger: flopsPerDollar fails to improve with Vera Rubin, or inference GPU demand growth stalls quarter over quarter.
entries.mechanism: Each NVIDIA generation lowers the cost to run a given inference job, so more applications become affordable and shift onto its GPUs.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether rival chips or custom silicon undercut NVIDIA's cost per token.
entries.statement: NVIDIA's each-generation drop in cost per token pulls more inference workloads onto its GPUs and widens the market it can serve.
entries.title: Cheaper inference pulls in demand

entries.falsifiableTrigger: A signed HBM take-or-pay deal (rpoBacklog) is canceled, or deposit-backed commitments fall below $22B within 4 quarters.
entries.mechanism: Buyers prepay billions under non-cancelable multi-year memory contracts, so a large share of future accelerator output is committed and paid for in advance.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether buyers honor deposits if AI demand cools.
entries.statement: Non-cancelable multi-year HBM contracts backed by billions in customer deposits lock a large share of future accelerator demand into place and reduce the chance that today's buildout is speculative.
entries.title: Prepaid HBM take-or-pay locks in accelerator demand

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Approved China license value (exportControlExposure) converts to booked revenue above $4,550M in a quarter, or the sub-50% cap is lifted.
entries.mechanism: US rules allow only case-by-case H200-class licenses capped below half of comparable US sales, so China access reopens but stays limited even as buyers line up.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether approved licenses turn into actual shipments and whether the cap moves.
entries.statement: China datacenter compute is reopening to NVIDIA only through case-by-case H200- and MI325-class licenses capped under half of comparable US sales, with Chinese buyers now signaling first purchases. This cycle adds H200-class licensing shifted from denial to case-by-case and buyer interest from Alibaba, ByteDance and DeepSeek, broadening the earlier MI325-only picture, while China revenue sits at $4,550M and H200 licenses have booked no revenue yet.
entries.title: Conditional China re-opening with a capped ceiling

entries.falsifiableTrigger: A major buyer migrates production inference off CUDA (market-share-pct shift), or ROCm deployments exceed a set share within 4 quarters.
entries.mechanism: Rivals like AMD's ROCm and domestic chips now run real training and inference, chipping at the software advantage that kept buyers on NVIDIA.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to how portable production AI software becomes across ROCm and custom chips.
entries.statement: The difficulty of running existing AI software on non-Nvidia chips keeps customers on Nvidia even when rivals cut hardware prices.
entries.title: CUDA software lock-in sustains the moat

entries.falsifiableTrigger: AI-server memory and NVMe costs (hbmSupplyCapex) stop rising or fall quarter over quarter as supply catches up.
entries.mechanism: Memory and NVMe shortages drive weekly price jumps in AI-server parts, raising the cost to build each server and pressuring buyer budgets and margins.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to when new memory capacity comes online relative to AI-server demand.
entries.statement: Fast-rising memory and NVMe prices are pushing up what it costs to build each AI server, which could strain buyer budgets and squeeze system margins.
entries.title: Rising memory costs inflate AI-server economics

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Any of the four ramps (releaseCadence) slips past H2 2026, or 2H26 output misses plan.
entries.mechanism: NVIDIA, AMD, AWS and Google are all pushing next-generation accelerators into mass production at the same time, adding to total supply in late 2026.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether shared memory and packaging supply can feed all four ramps at once.
entries.statement: A simultaneous mass-production ramp of NVIDIA, AMD, AWS, and Google accelerators is set to expand total accelerator supply in the second half of 2026.
entries.title: Multi-vendor accelerator supply wave in second-half 2026

entries.falsifiableTrigger: A single AMD design win (designWins) accounts for over 25% of DC GPU revenue, or a named mega-deal is canceled within 4 quarters.
entries.mechanism: A few very large commitments from Meta, OpenAI and cloud partners drive most of AMD's accelerator growth, so results hinge on keeping those specific deals.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether any one flagship partner delays or cancels its deployment.
entries.statement: AMD's data-center accelerator growth depends on a small set of very large commitments, which concentrates both its upside and its downside in a handful of partners.
entries.title: AMD growth leans on a few mega-deals

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Crescent Island sampling (releaseCadence) slips past 2H 2026, or LPDDR5X inference parts fail to reach volume within 4 quarters.
entries.mechanism: Intel's inference chip uses standard LPDDR5X memory instead of high-bandwidth memory, so it avoids the packaging and memory shortages that gate other accelerators.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether standard-memory parts deliver enough inference performance to attract buyers.
entries.statement: Intel's Crescent Island inference GPU uses standard LPDDR5X memory instead of high-bandwidth memory to sidestep the advanced-packaging and memory bottleneck, opening an alternative supply route for inference chips.
entries.title: Memory-based inference chips route around the packaging bottleneck

entries.falsifiableTrigger: TSMC gross margin (grossMargin) falls quarter over quarter, or CoWoS drops below full booking in 2026.
entries.mechanism: AI demand now spans GPUs, custom ASICs, networking and power chips, filling TSMC's capacity across nodes and letting it raise prices and margins.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether AI order breadth holds if any major buyer segment pulls back.
entries.statement: AI demand spreading across GPUs, custom ASICs, networking and power chips fills TSMC's capacity across nodes and lets it raise prices.
entries.title: Broadening AI demand tightens TSMC capacity and pricing

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Hyperscaler 2026 capex guidance (hyperscalerCapexRevision) is cut quarter over quarter, or a top hyperscaler announces an AI capex reduction.
entries.mechanism: Hyperscalers are raising AI capital spending far faster than proven returns, so disappointing payback could trigger a pullback that cuts accelerator orders.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether AI revenue growth catches up to the capital being deployed.
entries.statement: Hyperscalers' sharp jump in AI capital spending risks a pullback if returns disappoint, which would cut accelerator orders.
entries.title: Hyperscaler AI spending may outrun near-term returns

entries.falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA non-GAAP gross margin (grossMargin) falls below 70% in a quarter during the Rubin ramp.
entries.mechanism: Buyers keep paying premium prices for NVIDIA GPUs, so it holds gross margin near 75% even while ramping new products, far above rivals.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether competition or costs force NVIDIA to discount as new chips ramp.
entries.statement: NVIDIA keeps its gross margin near three-quarters even while ramping new products, far above rivals, showing buyers still pay premium prices.
entries.title: NVIDIA holds a premium gross margin as it ramps new chips

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Top-three CoWoS customerConcentration falls below 85%, or a fourth buyer takes double-digit share within 4 quarters.
entries.mechanism: A few buyers led by NVIDIA book most of TSMC's advanced-packaging output, so any one cutting orders would leave capacity that is hard to refill.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether a new large packaging buyer emerges to diversify the base.
entries.statement: A few AI chip buyers control most of TSMC's advanced-packaging output, so any one of them cutting orders would leave capacity that is hard to refill.
entries.title: AI packaging supply is concentrated in a few buyers

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Contracted backlog value (rpoBacklog) shrinks quarter over quarter, or new commitments shorten below one year.
entries.mechanism: Clouds and chip suppliers keep signing multi-year purchase deals, so a growing share of AI compute demand is locked in years before delivery.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether long-dated commitments hold if AI demand softens.
entries.statement: Cloud and chip suppliers are signing longer-dated purchase commitments that push out the average life of their order books, so a growing share of AI compute demand is booked years in advance.
entries.title: Backlog duration lengthens as demand is booked years ahead

entries.falsifiableTrigger: A leading model provider reports revenue (apiArr) growth stalling quarter over quarter while compute commitments keep growing.
entries.mechanism: Model providers fund their heavy compute spending out of their own sales, so the buildout is only durable if those sales keep rising.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether model providers disclose rising revenue rather than just larger compute commitments.
entries.statement: Leading AI model providers are growing revenue fast enough that their heavy compute spending rests on real and rising sales rather than hope.
entries.title: Model-provider revenue scales to underpin the buildout

entries.falsifiableTrigger: A flagship Chinese model still needs smuggled NVIDIA GPUs (exportControlExposure), or domestic-ASIC clusters fail to scale past 50,000 chips within 4 quarters.
entries.mechanism: Chinese firms are training frontier-scale models on tens of thousands of domestic accelerators, so some Chinese AI compute no longer depends on imported NVIDIA GPUs.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether domestic chips can match NVIDIA on memory and software at scale.
entries.statement: China's home-grown AI accelerators are starting to train large models without NVIDIA chips, cutting the country's need for imported GPUs.
entries.title: China Domestic Accelerators Displace Banned NVIDIA GPUs

entries.falsifiableTrigger: A major neocloud posts a net profit, or its contracted backlog (rpoBacklog) falls quarter over quarter.
entries.mechanism: Neoclouds like CoreWeave book fast-rising revenue and huge backlogs but spend heavily on GPUs and debt, so their net losses widen even as sales grow.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether rental revenue can cover GPU depreciation and financing costs.
entries.statement: Fast-growing neocloud GPU buyers such as CoreWeave are booking record revenue while their net losses widen.
entries.title: Neocloud GPU Buyers Grow Revenue but Deepen Losses

entries.falsifiableTrigger: AI buildouts stop being sized in gigawatts, or planned power capacity growth stalls for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: Each new AI cluster needs large dedicated power and cooling, so limited grid and site capacity slows how quickly bought accelerators can be switched on.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to how fast utilities and developers can add power and cooling to sites.
entries.statement: Companies now size and cap their AI buildouts by gigawatts of available power, so electricity and site capacity increasingly limit how many accelerators they can actually deploy.
entries.title: Power capacity is becoming the binding limit on AI buildout

entries.falsifiableTrigger: A third co-design vendor wins a major custom-AI-chip program, or the two-firm share falls below 80% within 4 quarters.
entries.mechanism: Designing a competitive AI accelerator needs rare co-design skill held mostly by two firms, so hyperscalers depend on them to build the chips that replace merchant GPUs.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether hyperscalers build in-house design teams or a third co-design vendor emerges.
entries.statement: Hyperscalers' shift to custom AI chips runs almost entirely through two outside design firms, so the alternative to merchant GPUs is itself concentrated in those two suppliers.
entries.title: The custom-AI-chip alternative depends on two design houses
